Leonardo, it is Diane. I am calling from the car park, so this will be quick, and I wanted you to hear it today and not in an email next week. You were good in there. I have watched about forty of these presentations and I am going to tell you exactly what happened, because you will not have seen it yourself. First, you opened with the recommendation and you did not apologize for it. Nobody in that room knew it was your first board in English, and I promise you nobody wondered. Second, the moment that decided it. Our finance director interrupted you at minute four, which he always does, and you did not lose the thread. You said let me come back to that in one minute and then you actually came back to it. That is the thing people cannot fake. Third, and this is the part I want you to write down. When he pushed on the eleven percent, you hedged properly. You said in our view, and you said there might be, and you did not overstate a single number. A lawyer who overstates on a first presentation never gets a second one. Now the honest part, because you will ask me. You still speed up when you are nervous, and twice you ran three sentences together where a pause would have done more work than any of the words. That is not English. That is delivery, and you can fix it in a month. The board wants the full mandate. I am sending the paperwork on Monday, and I told them you would be leading it.

I run the international desk at a firm in London, and every year I watch people finish a language program and then quietly lose most of it, so let me tell you what separates the ones who keep it. It is not talent and it is not more classes. It is three habits, and none of them takes more than twenty minutes a week. The first one is that you have to use it before you feel ready. The single biggest predictor of whether somebody still speaks well in a year is whether they took a call in English in the first month after their course ended. Not a perfect call. Any call. If you wait until you feel ready, the language cools down, and cold language is much harder to restart than tired language. The second habit is that you keep one live thing. One podcast you actually finish, one client relationship where the working language is English, one newsletter you read on a Monday. One. People who try to keep five keep zero. The third one is the exam, and I am going to be blunt about it. Book the date before you feel prepared. A date on a calendar organizes the whole year behind it, and the version of you who is preparing for a real exam in November studies differently from the version who intends to take one eventually. Everything you have built is still yours next week. Whether it is still yours next year is decided by what you do in the next thirty days.
